text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementNeuroscienceThe Myth of Mommy BrainA conversation with neuroscientist Susana Carmona, author of “A Mother’s Brain,” about how the brain changes in motherhoodKFBy Kristen French1:00 PM CST on November 4, 2026Add Nautilus to Google“Science must begin with myths, and with the criticism of the myths,” reads the very first sentence of Susana Carmona’s new book A Mother’s Brain. The line is borrowed from Conjectures and Refutations, a foundational work in the philosophy of science published in 1963 by Karl Popper. Carmona picks up the gauntlet. She begins with the tenacious myth that mothers’ brains turn to mush the moment a baby begins to grow in their wombs, a cognitive fog that stretches into their final years. Then she spends the rest of the book complicating and reframing it.For nearly two decades, Carmona, a neuroscientist, has been studying how motherhood remodels the female brain.
